title: 米中間選挙「MAGA」の動向焦点
body:
米中間選挙が１１月３日に投開票される。２０２５年１月に就任し、「米国第一」の政策を掲げたトランプ大統領に米国民が審判を下す場になる。結果は今後の政権運営にも大きな影響を及ぼす。中間選挙の仕組みや今回の焦点などを解説する。【地図】上院選の「接戦の構図」
４年ごとに実施される大統領選の中間の年に、上下両院の議員や州知事などを一斉に決めるのが「中間選挙」だ。大統領選と同じ「１１月第１月曜日の次の火曜日」に行われることが連邦法で定められている。農業に従事する人が多かった時代の名残で、収穫期が終わり、本格的な冬が到来する前の１１月としている。火曜日は、キリスト教徒が教会に行く日曜を避け、月曜に馬車で投票所まで移動することを想定したものとされる。
大統領自身は出馬しないが、現政権に対する評価を問う「中間テスト」と位置づけられている。今回はトランプ大統領を熱烈に支持する「ＭＡＧＡ（マガ）」と呼ばれる人たちの動向などが注目される。
与党の共和党が負ければ、議会では与野党が対立するテーマの法案で共和党が大きな譲歩を余儀なくされる可能性があり、政権は重視する政策を進めることが難しくなる。トランプ氏の求心力低下は避けられず、２年後の大統領選の行方にも影響する。
州全体が一つの選挙区となっている上院（任期６年、定数１００）は２年ごとに３分の１ずつが改選される。今回は補欠選挙を含めた３５議席が対象となる。
下院（任期２年、定数４３５議席）は全議席が改選対象だ。議席数は、各州にまず１議席を割り当てた後、残りの３８５議席を人口規模に応じて配分している。最多のカリフォルニア州は５２議席で、アラスカ州やデラウェア州など６州は１議席のみとなっている。
各党は中間選挙に向け、それぞれ予備選挙を実施する。党内で候補者が競い合い、勝った方が１１月の本選挙に臨む。現職でも予備選挙に負ければ本選挙に進めなくなる。
共和党は今年の予備選で、トランプ氏が支持した候補が現職を相次ぎ破り、注目された。トランプ氏のスローガン「米国を再び偉大に」の頭文字をとった「ＭＡＧＡ」の影響力の大きさを示した。野党の民主党では、上院選の一部で急進左派の支援を受けた候補が党主流派の推す候補との戦いを制した。本選での勝敗が急進左派全体の勢いを示すこととなり、民主党の今後の方向性に影響を与えそうだ。

title: 阪神高速でトラック横転 単独か
body:
けさ＝3日朝、阪神高速・1号環状線の本町出口付近でトラックが横転する事故がありました。【関連ニュース画像】秋に事故が多くなる理由とは阪神高速によると、3日午前10時半現在、付近では車線規制が実施されているほか、上り線の高麗橋入口が封鎖されています。
警察によると、トラックは単独事故で横転したとみられ、運転手は意識があり、命に別状はないとみられます。この事故の影響で1号環状線では、北浜出口付近を先頭に2キロの渋滞が発生し、周辺の阪神高速12号守口線の上り・南森町入口付近を先頭に4キロの渋滞が起きています。守口線では、上りの長柄と都島の入り口が閉鎖されています。

title: 親と縁切る「家族じまい」相談増
body:
親子の縁を断ち切る『家族じまい』の相談が急増しています。以前は高齢者の問題が主でしたが、現在は20代や30代からの依頼が増加しています。壮絶な体験談や“老い逃げ”という言葉から、浮き彫りになる複雑な家族関係と代行サービスの実態とは。【ニュースto】｢高すぎる｣｢芸術に惜しみなく使うべき｣鎌倉市が税金で約4400万円の“高級ピアノ”を買い替え決定で物議…市長｢公共的な意義がある｣
親の介護ができない、あるいは親族との関わりを断ちたいといった理由から、現在『家族じまい』についての相談を寄せる家庭が多くなっています。特に、20代から30代の若い世代からの問い合わせが急増している状況です。そもそも、皆さんにとって『家族』とはどのような存在でしょうか。Q.あなたにとって『家族』とは？（街の人）「戻ってくる場所じゃないですけど、安心できるものではあるかな」「やっぱりありがたいです。仕事終わって家に帰って（家族に）会えると、なんかちょっとホッとします」このように、安心感を与えてくれる、帰るべき場所として家族を捉える声がある一方で、親子などの縁を完全に断ち切り、関係を終わらせる『家族じまい』を選ぶケースが増加しています。切っても切れない家族の縁を、なぜ自ら断ち切ろうとするのでしょうか。
こちらの60代の男性は、実際に『家族じまい』を行ったその一人です。幼少期に父親を亡くし、女手一つで育ててくれた母親と縁を切る決断をしました。その背景には壮絶なものがありました。男性は約30年前に結婚し、妻と3人の子ども、そして自身の母親と同居生活を送っていました。しかし、次第に妻と母親の間で嫁姑（よめしゅうとめ）問題が生じ始めます。
男性は最終的に母親だけを残して別居することになりましたが、1人で生活する母親を放っておけないと心配し、月に数回のペースで実家へ足を運んでいました。ところが、訪問のたびに母親から妻に対する不満だけでなく、“男性の妻の浮気”を疑い始めました。しかし、その疑念の理由は信じがたいものでした。（60代男性）「私は27歳ぐらいから髪の毛が薄くなって、父も、祖父もハゲなんです。長男だけはハゲない。それを見て、『お前の子じゃない』『お前の女房が浮気した時の子なんだ』と」

title: 鳥山明さん仕事場解体へ 惜しむ声
body: 世界的人気漫画・アニメ「ドラゴンボール」などの作者で、2024年に亡くなった漫画家の鳥山明さんが仕事場としてきた愛知県清須市内の建物の解体工事が進んでいる。数々の名作を生んだ「聖地」の消失に、地元や関係者からは惜しむ声が上がっている。【写真で見る】いまの「聖地」の様子は…？清須市出身の鳥山さんは長年、市内の自宅を仕事場としてきた。黄色の外観が特徴的で、地元住民やファンらの間では聖地として有名だった。所属会社「バード・スタジオ」もこの建物に置かれていたが、24年3月に68歳で亡くなった後、26年8月に清須市から東京に移転。残された建物の行く末が注目されていた。工事は10月に始まり、既に大部分が取り壊されている。◇「記憶の中で残っていけば」現場を見に行ったという鳥山さんの元アシスタントでイラストレーターのまつやまたかしさん（68）は「鳥山さんの作品のほとんどはそこから生まれている。自分の働いていた場所でもあり悲しい」と振り返る。その上で「住宅街なので博物館にするというのも難しかったと思うし、仕方ない。記憶の中で残っていけば」と語った。近所の60代女性は「穏やかな先生で動物がすごく好きだった」と鳥山さんとの交流を懐かしみ、「外国人もよく見に来ていた。市のシンボルだったのでもったいない」と解体を惜しんだ。SNSでもファンの間で解体が話題となっており、「先生の職場が無くなるのはつらい」「創作拠点は、日本だけでなく世界の漫画文化にとって重要な場所」などといったコメントが相次いでいる。永田純夫市長は毎日新聞の取材に「取り壊しは鳥山先生のご家族によって決定されたものと拝察する。市としてはご意向を尊重し、静謐（せいひつ）な環境で工事が完了することを見守りたい」とコメントした。【川瀬慎一朗】

title: 米中間選挙「MAGA」の動向焦点
body:
米中間選挙が１１月３日に投開票される。２０２５年１月に就任し、「米国第一」の政策を掲げたトランプ大統領に米国民が審判を下す場になる。結果は今後の政権運営にも大きな影響を及ぼす。中間選挙の仕組みや今回の焦点などを解説する。【地図】上院選の「接戦の構図」
４年ごとに実施される大統領選の中間の年に、上下両院の議員や州知事などを一斉に決めるのが「中間選挙」だ。大統領選と同じ「１１月第１月曜日の次の火曜日」に行われることが連邦法で定められている。農業に従事する人が多かった時代の名残で、収穫期が終わり、本格的な冬が到来する前の１１月としている。火曜日は、キリスト教徒が教会に行く日曜を避け、月曜に馬車で投票所まで移動することを想定したものとされる。
大統領自身は出馬しないが、現政権に対する評価を問う「中間テスト」と位置づけられている。今回はトランプ大統領を熱烈に支持する「ＭＡＧＡ（マガ）」と呼ばれる人たちの動向などが注目される。
与党の共和党が負ければ、議会では与野党が対立するテーマの法案で共和党が大きな譲歩を余儀なくされる可能性があり、政権は重視する政策を進めることが難しくなる。トランプ氏の求心力低下は避けられず、２年後の大統領選の行方にも影響する。
州全体が一つの選挙区となっている上院（任期６年、定数１００）は２年ごとに３分の１ずつが改選される。今回は補欠選挙を含めた３５議席が対象となる。
下院（任期２年、定数４３５議席）は全議席が改選対象だ。議席数は、各州にまず１議席を割り当てた後、残りの３８５議席を人口規模に応じて配分している。最多のカリフォルニア州は５２議席で、アラスカ州やデラウェア州など６州は１議席のみとなっている。
各党は中間選挙に向け、それぞれ予備選挙を実施する。党内で候補者が競い合い、勝った方が１１月の本選挙に臨む。現職でも予備選挙に負ければ本選挙に進めなくなる。
共和党は今年の予備選で、トランプ氏が支持した候補が現職を相次ぎ破り、注目された。トランプ氏のスローガン「米国を再び偉大に」の頭文字をとった「ＭＡＧＡ」の影響力の大きさを示した。野党の民主党では、上院選の一部で急進左派の支援を受けた候補が党主流派の推す候補との戦いを制した。本選での勝敗が急進左派全体の勢いを示すこととなり、民主党の今後の方向性に影響を与えそうだ。

title: トランプ氏 演説で「口約束」連発
body: 【ワシントン時事】トランプ米大統領が、中間選挙を前に焦りを募らせている。上院激戦州での演説で、支持拡大を狙う「口約束」を連発。会場では歓声が上がるものの、有権者にどこまで響いているかは疑問符が付く。【ひと目でわかる】28年大統領選候補として取り沙汰される3氏共和党は、長らく牙城としてきた中西部のアイオワ、カンザス両州などで苦戦を強いられている。選挙戦最終盤の1日、トランプ氏は両州で演説。中東情勢の悪化で高騰する燃料価格を抑制するため、エタノール混合ガソリンの通年販売を「アイオワで（共和党候補が）上院議員になれば恒久化する」と語り、支持を呼び掛けた。コンバインなどに使われる軽油が記録的な高値で推移する中、トランプ氏は10月中旬にカンザス州で、収穫期の農家の負担を軽減するため、80億ドル（約1兆2600億円）の支援制度を始めると表明した。ただ、政権高官は米メディアに対し、支給は中間選挙後になると言明。収穫期までに農家の手元に届くわけではなく、直ちに恩恵があるとは言い難い。バンス副大統領の地元であるオハイオ州でさえ、現有議席の確保に躍起になっている。トランプ氏は、共和党上院候補が勝利すれば、新設する「宇宙アカデミー」を同州に置くことを「検討する」と約束した。トランプ氏はこれまで、「大統領でいると少しだけ有利だという理由が、今は分かる」と語ってきた。だが、1日公表された米NBCニュースの10月末の調査によると、共和党支持者の53％が経済面での現状に不満を表明。トランプ氏が「約束を果たしていない」と答えたのは37％に上った。

title: 米・露・ウが10～11日に3者協議
body: Steve Holland［ワシントン　２日　ロイター］ - 米国のウィットコフ和平交渉担当特使は２日、米国とロシア、‌ウクライナの３カ国による実務者協議を１０─１１日⁠にアラブ首長国連邦（ＵＡＥ）のアブダビで開くと明らかにした。「戦後の安全保障協定、緊​張緩和、人道支援措置、戦争の終結」を議題にするとソーシャルメディ‌アで述べた。ロシアのプーチン大統領は２週間前にサンクトペテルブルクでウィトコフ氏と‌会談した際、新たな３者協‌議の開催に合意した。米国は、本格​的な冬の到来を前に、長期化する紛争の打開を目‌指している。米国が仲介した前回の和平交渉は、米国とイスラ‌エルがイランへの​攻撃を開始する前の２月に行われた。米高官は、‌今回のアブダビ協議で、ウィットコフ氏とトランプ大⁠統領の娘婿ジャレッド・クシュナー氏が出席する予定だと述べた。今週、米交渉団は、ブリュッセルで⁠フランス、ドイツ、英国、欧州​連合（ＥＵ）、北大西‌洋条約機構（ＮＡＴＯ）との実務者会合を開き、「ウクライナの安全の保証、欧州の将来の安全保障枠組み、⁠ウクライナ復興に向けた経済支援」に⁠ついて協議する。高官は、これらの会合は関係国間の最近⁠の議論を踏まえたものであり、「ロシアとウクライナの間‌で永⁠続的な和平合意を実現するためのトランプ米​大統領による継続的な取り組みを反映したものだ」と述べた。

title: 露軍がウの学校に空爆 26人死亡
body:
ロシアによる侵略が続くウクライナの非常事態当局は２日、同国南部ザポリージャ州コミシュバハの学校が露軍の空爆を受け、少なくとも２６人が死亡し、５人が負傷したと発表した。標的となった学校は、人道支援物資を配布する拠点として利用されていた。【写真】「核攻撃を警告」緊急警報用アプリが偽情報配信
ウクライナのウォロディミル・ゼレンスキー大統領は２日、ＳＮＳへの投稿で「ロシアが事態の沈静化も、真の正義も望んでいないことを裏付けるものだ」と批判した。ゼレンスキー氏によると最初の空爆後、人々が避難していたシェルターを狙ってさらに９発の爆弾が落とされたという。
両国は、露軍の占領下で孤立したウクライナ南部ヘルソン州オレシュキでの人道支援活動と住民退避のため、１日まで局地的な停戦を続けていた。

title: GMO熊谷社長ら 報酬を3カ月減額
body:
ＧＭＯインターネットのＦＸ（外国為替証拠金）取引用クラウドサービスが不正アクセスを受け、利用者とみられる個人情報が公開された問題で、同社は２日、親会社のＧＭＯインターネットグループの熊谷正寿会長兼社長ら４人の役員報酬を減額すると発表した。【一覧】サイバー攻撃で個人情報などの流出が判明した企業・団体
熊谷氏は月額報酬の３０％を３か月、ＧＭＯインターネットの伊藤正社長は月額報酬の２５％を３か月の減額とする。今年１２月分から減額する。

title: フラット35 金利3.81%で過去2番目
body: 住宅金融支援機構は2日、最長35年間、金利を固定する住宅ローン「フラット35」の11月分の適用金利を発表した。住宅購入価格に対する借入額が9割以下で適用される最低金利は年3.810%となり、4カ月ぶりに下がった。ただ、制度改正があった2017年10月1日以降で、今年10月分に続いて2番目に高い。【家計破綻】「ぜいたくしてない」40歳課長→50歳部長でも…住宅ローン返せず11月分の適用金利は、10月分の3.830%から0.02%幅下落した。フラット35の適用金利は、前月の長期金利の利回りと連動しており、10月の長期金利は、AI関連銘柄を中心とする日米の株安を受けて、投資家の間に国債に資金を移す動きが広がったため、上昇が一服していた。下がったとはいえ、3%を超えるのは6カ月連続。昨年末まで1%台だったことを踏まえると、なお高水準が続いている。（小川聡仁）

title: SBIとフジHDが資本業務提携 発表
body: ［東京　２日　ロイター］ - ＳＢＩホールディングス、ＳＢＩネ‌オメディアホール⁠ディングスとフジ・メディア・​ホールディングスは２日、メディア‌・コンテンツ領域で資本業務提‌携契約を締結‌したと発表し​た。両グループの折半‌出資で合弁会社を２７年１月に設立する。‌合弁会​社はコンテンツや‌知的財産（ＩＰ）を起点に、⁠ライブ・イベント等を通じ顧客との関⁠係を育む「リ​アル・メ‌ディア」を中枢とし、将来的には複数事⁠業への展開を⁠見据えた持ち株会社と⁠する。両社は今年６月、戦略的業務‌提携⁠に向けた協議を開​始したと発表していた。

title: 安いもやし限界 5年で13社消える
body:
「家計の味方」として食卓を支える「もやし」業界の苦戦が続いている。2026年に「もやし」製造業者の倒産や休廃業・解散（以下、廃業）は少なくとも3件判明し、10月に事業を停止した「サイキ食品」（埼玉）を含めると4件となった。過去5年間（2022～26年）に倒産・廃業となったもやし製造業者は計13件に達する。ただ、小規模事業者も多く、水面下の撤退を含めれば、実際にはさらに多くの製造業者が市場から姿を消したとみられる。もやし業界では、以前から販売価格が「安すぎる」問題が指摘されてきた。2017年には工業組合もやし生産者協会が業界の窮状を訴える声明を公表したほか、原料豆卸の「大西商事」（2017年11月、破産）が価格転嫁できず経営破綻し、業界の厳しい実情が注目された。2022年には同協会が日本経済新聞に「このままでは生産者が消える」とする全面広告を掲載。ロシアのウクライナ侵攻を契機とする物価高を背景に価格改定は進んだものの、「もやしは安くて当然」という認識を大きく変えるには至らなかった。こうしたなか、2026年10月には埼玉県を中心にもやしを生産・出荷していた大手のサイキ食品が事業を停止した。
足元でもコスト上昇圧力は強い。財務省貿易統計によると、もやしの主原料である緑豆の輸入単価は2026年1～8月平均で前年同期比7.2％上昇した。原料豆に加え、包装資材や電力などのエネルギーコスト、物流費、人件費も上昇が続き、業績面でも影響を及ぼしている。「もやし製造」を主力とする企業のうち、2025年度業績が判明した全国約20社では約3割が最終赤字となった。さらに減益企業を含めると、全体の65％、3社に2社で業績が悪化した。業績悪化企業の割合は2021年度（75.0％）をピークに改善傾向が続いていたが、2025年度は4年ぶりに前年を上回った。他の野菜価格が高騰するなかでも、節約志向を背景にもやし需要そのものは底堅く推移している。しかし、コスト増を十分に価格へ転嫁できず、「売れているのに儲からない」状態に陥る製造業者は少なくない。利益を確保している企業でも、健康志向を背景に単価の高いスプラウトや、カット野菜・ミックス野菜などを併営し、もやし単体の低収益を補うケースが目立ち、もやしだけでは利益を確保しづらい構造は変わっていない。もやしは地域密着型の生産体制が多く、1社の撤退でも供給網に影響を及ぼしかねない。「安くて当然」を前提とした販売構造から脱却できなければ、生産者の減少は今後も続く可能性がある。「このままでは将来、価格が高騰する」というかつての警鐘は、価格の問題にとどまらず、安定供給そのものが維持できなくなる懸念に及びつつある。

title: 子どものセルフレジ操作 SNS賛否
body: スーパーなどのお買い物で、すっかりおなじみとなった「セルフレジ」。店舗の省人化やスピーディーな会計に一役買っている一方で、ある光景をめぐりSNS上で激しい議論が巻き起こっています。【写真を見る】セルフレジで“ピッ”　操作を子どもにやらせるのはアリ?ナシ?　「レジはおもちゃじゃない」「無理にやめさせたらギャン泣き」親の配慮不足?寛容さが足りない?SNSで賛否議論「混雑しているレジで、子どもに1品ずつスキャンさせている親、勘弁してほしい」Threads（スレッズ）やX（旧Twitter）などのSNS上では、こうした「子どものセルフレジ操作」に対する不満や批判が定期的に投稿され、そのたびに「共感」と「反論」が入り乱れる議論が巻き起こっています。不快感を露わにする利用者がいる一方で、育児中の親たちにも切実な事情がある模様。この問題の背景と、現場の双方の主張とは?■批判派の不満「セルフレジは教育の場ではない」セルフレジの「子ども操作」に否定的な声をあげる人々の多くは、特に「混雑時の時間ロス」を指摘しています。「後ろに長蛇の列ができているのに、親がニコニコ見守りながら子どもにゆっくりスキャンさせているのを見るとイライラする」「セルフレジはスピード重視の場所。お金の勉強や社会体験ならお店が空いている時間帯にやってほしい」「レジはおもちゃじゃない。例え混雑していないとしてもやらせるべきじゃない」ネット上では「職業体験アトラクションと勘違いしていないか」「自分だけの世界に入り込んでいる親の配慮不足」といった厳しい声が目立ちます。■親側の苦悩「やめさせると、その場で大惨事に…」一方で、育児中の親たちからは「決して好きでやらせているわけではない」という声も…。「子どもが自分でやりたがる年頃は、無理に止めさせるとその場でひっくり返ってギャン泣き（癇癪）を起こす」「泣き叫ぶ子どもを抱えて会計する方が、結果的に周りに迷惑がかかるし時間もかかる」実際に小さなお子さんを育てながら日常的にスーパーを利用している母親に話を聞いてみると…── 混雑時に子どもが「自分でセルフレジをやりたい」と言い出したとき、どのように対応していますか?

title: Russian bombing kills 26 people at Ukraine aid centre, Kyiv says
summary: Officials say at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit a southern Ukrainian village in what the president called an "utterly horrific" attack.
body:
Video shows smoke rising from Komyshuvakha blast crater
At least 26 people were killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre, in an attack that Ukraine's leader has called "utterly horrific".
Five people were injured and 27 initially reported missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering.
He posteda video showing a huge crater left after Monday's attack, and rescuer teams searching through the rubble.
The Russian military has not publicly commented.
There are fears that the death toll will rise further as a number of people are still under the rubble
Zelensky initially put the death toll at 18, but Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS later said 24 people, including two rescuers and four police officers, were confirmed to have been killed.
In his video address late on Monday, Zelensky said 26 people were now known to have died.
He earlier said that "the Russians could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week" on Monday.
"This is yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation."
He said that after a recent successful joint Russian-Ukrainian operation to evacuate civilians from the Russia-occupied southern city of Oleshky during a temporary ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump,"there was a moment when the next steps could show that peace is possible".
"With such killings, Russia is sending the exact opposite signal - Russia is counting on further killings," Zelensky said.
The Russian strikes left a huge crater where Ukrainian officials say people were sheltering
Meanwhile, Semikin described the Russian attack as a "terrible tragedy" for the village, confirming that "people are still under the rubble".
He said rescue teams were working at the scene, but they had been forced to halt their operation a number of times because of Russian drone attacks in the area.
A day of mourning has been declared for Tuesday across the entire Zaporizhzhia region.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Teams from Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to resume peace talks in Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates, next week, US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff said on X.
Since the talks were suspended in February, Moscow has stepped up attacks as Kyiv virtually ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.
No major breakthrough is expected at the talks. Witkoff said the discussions would focus on "post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace".
Witkoff said US negotiators would also meet European and Nato officials this week in Brussels.

title: Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace
summary: Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in any offensive operations.
body:
A British paratrooper takes part in a previous Nato training exercise less than 50km (31 miles) from the Russian border in Finland
Britain and France are to lead a military exercise to test a multinational force's ability to deploy to Ukraine, if there is a peace deal.
Nearly 3,000 military personnel from 12 European nations will take part in the rehearsal in neighbouring Poland this month.
Plans for a reassurance force for Ukraine were set out last year as one of the long-term security guarantees being proposed by European nations.
But there are still more questions than answers as to how such a military force might work in practice. Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in offensive operations or be involved in peacekeeping or ceasefire monitoring missions.
Nor would they be operating under the command of Nato or on the front line.
Officials say their presence would be to provide reassurance to Ukraine and to help rebuild its armed forces.
The US has been involved in discussions, but is not contributing to the mission.
Russia has already voiced opposition to foreign troops being stationed in Ukraine and, last year, President Vladimir Putin said they would be "legitimate targets".
Western officials have declined to spell out the rules of engagement if any international troops were to be attacked in Ukraine. Though they say the force would be able to defend itself.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the exercise showed Britain, France and their allies were stepping up preparation for the day when peace came to Ukraine.
He said: "This is not a hypothetical plan, it's a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops."
Lt Gen Tom Bateman, the UK commander of the Multi National Force – Ukraine (MNF-U), said the exercise represented an important step in translating political commitments into credible military readiness.
He said it was a "real, capable, readily deployable force that represented a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine's long-term stability and security".
Ukrainian troops take part in urban warfare training at a military base in England in 2023
Exercise Koalicja - which takes place from 9-22 November - will be a rehearsal of how to move, protect and supply a force in Ukraine. It will also be a test of their command and control to ensure troops from different countries can work together.
Some 2,800 military personnel will take part across land, sea and air, with the UK contribution including 300 troops and a pair of RAF Typhoons.
Fighter jets will simulate how they would reassure commercial aircraft once Ukraine's skies can be reopened.
Turkey has agreed to lead the maritime mission, with the eventual goal to clear mines and allow the resumption of trade in the Black Sea.
As well as the UK, troops will come from France, Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and Turkey.
However, Western officials could not comment on the final make-up and shape of the force that could be deployed to Ukraine if the fighting stops.
In the past, military experts have suggested that Western nations might have to send tens of thousands of troops to Ukraine to guarantee its security.
Officials acknowledge that the countries' commitment and contributions will depend on the circumstances of a cessation of hostilities and individual nations' political decisions.
It is also unclear what training role Western forces could provide to battle hardened Ukraine.
Ukrainian soldiers are already in high demand training Nato forces - passing on their expertise in drone warfare.
Above all, Russia has shown no sign of wanting to end its war.

title: Plane may have broken apart ahead of deadly Florida jet crash, say investigators
summary: The National Transportation Safety Board also believes weather could have been a factor in the crash, but warns it is too early to determine the cause.
body:
Dashcam footage captures Florida private jet crash
The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) says it will investigate  whether parts of a jet that crashed in Florida broke off before it nose-dived and exploded, killing all nine people on board.
The Learjet 60, which was travelling from Austin, Texas to the Bahamas on Sunday, crashed on a street nine miles (14 km) from President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort.
A tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old copilot, were among those who died.
The NTSB said on Monday that it would also investigate to what extent ice and turbulence may have been contributing factors.
Final moments before deadly Florida plane crash
It confirmed that, after the jet took off from Austin, the crew transmitted to air traffic control that they were encountering ice and moderate turbulence.
"We are picking up precipitation, requesting to climb to 37,000 feet if able," the crew said.
NTSB member Tom Chapman said that less than 30 seconds later, the plane began to descend and the crew issued a mayday call.
The transmission then became "unintelligible", he said, adding that: "Sadly, all aboard were lost."
The NTSB said that ice and turbulence were factors in the crash but that determining its probable cause will be a "lengthy investigatory process".
Thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time.
Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was on board at the time of the crash and if it can be recovered.
As part of the investigation, the NTSB is working with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), representatives from Learjet as well as meteorologists and air traffic control experts.
Recovering the wreckage from the crater on the roadway will be a "daunting challenge", said Timothy Monville, an air safety investigator with the safety board.
Officials describe how Learjet flight unfolded before deadly crash
Flight analysis indicates the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before crashing.
In air traffic control audio, a crew member can be heard declaring an emergency, shouting "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".
About 35 seconds after the initial mayday announcement, the last remark from the cockpit appears to be "we're out of time".
The seven people killed who were travelling as passengers were identified in a joint statement from their families as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma and Charlie - as well as Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina.
The pilot was named in media reports as Jeffery Gregory, while Nathalia Filgueiras, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the copilot.
As well as those killed, one man on the ground sustained a leg injury when the plane nosedived onto the street.
Who are the victims of the deadly Florida jet crash?
The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said the crash happened on Military Trail, a six-lane road lined with businesses and restaurants.
Images from the crash scene show a large fiery crater in the middle of a residential suburban street.
The debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area, officials told a news conference on Monday, possible evidence that the plane broke up before it hit the ground.
Unverified footage posted on social media shows what appears to be a dash-camera recording of the moment of the crash.
Trump was at Mar-a-Lago on Sunday morning, and departed from an airport nearby on Air Force One about an hour before the crash.

title: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
summary: The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C.
body:
'All this food is now useless': Piles of rubbish after shop freezers hit by cyber-attack
Dozens of supermarkets across sevenEuropean countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incidentthat hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.
Freezers have had to be emptied at several ICA grocery stores in Sweden after the cyber-attack
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".
He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.
Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.
"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.
The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).
It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.
In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.
Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.
In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost €100,000 (£83,500) worth of produce.
The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.
Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".
An employee at an ICA supermarket in Sweden's capital Stockholm was pictured throwing away bags of spoiled food
In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit.
A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".
"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.
One of the ICA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."
The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.
Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.
In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores.
The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.
The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.
In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.
A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.
A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.

title: Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire
summary: Though unprecedented, the six-day truce has done little to alter the wider trajectory of a war that continues to grinds on.
body:
Hundreds of Oleshky evacuees arrived back in Ukraine on Saturday after years trapped on the frontline
Fighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the front-line region for the first time in years.
The ceasefire - the longest since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - allowed hundreds of people trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky and its surroundings to be evacuated.
On Monday morning, local authorities confirmed that strikes had resumed, saying Moscow had hit a medical facility in Kherson city centre. They also said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were injured when a Russian drone attacked the car they were travelling in.
Ukraine also accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian ceasefire to strengthen their military positions, rotate units and deliver ammunition.
"The enemy used the humanitarian pause to set up their positions," said Ukraine's General Staff, adding they had recorded rotation of Russian units, expansion of anti-drone equipment on the roads, and delivery of ammunition.
The Kremlin appeared to corroborate this when spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was "reasonable to assume that the Ukrainian army also used this period for the necessary regrouping".
"It is a completely standard practice in such situations," he added.
The ceasefire had been brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Both Kyiv and Moscow thanked her repeatedly, though no details of her involvement were shared.
An unusual show of cooperation came from Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets. The pair oversaw the ceasefire, travelled into Oleshky and were filmed speaking to residents together. They publicly thanked each other for their work, often highlighting that no violations of the ceasefire had been observed.
Both Lantratova and Lubinets called for the initiative to be repeated elsewhere, and Ukraine repeatedly said it would be prepared to observe similar ceasefires on a national level too.
But many have questioned whether this will lead to more cooperation and further truces.
In fact, the Kremlin swiftly dismissed the idea even as the ceasefire was under way, calling Oleshky "an isolated case" which would not affect the "settlement process" – a euphemism for the stalled peace talks. "There are no similar plans or initiatives," Peskov reiterated on Monday.
And although last week the guns fell silent in Kherson region, elsewhere in Ukraine Russia's air strikes continued, killing scores of civilians and destroying crucial infrastructure.
The decision to observe an unusually broad and comparatively lengthy ceasefire in and around Oleshky was therefore a notable exception.
The ceasefire's observance appears, at least in part, to have been linked to Melania Trump's reported involvement. By violating the truce, Moscow would have risked undermining its own efforts to cultivate the crucial relationship with her husband, US President Donald Trump.
Some commentators have argued that Trump himself would be interested in presenting the Oleshky ceasefire as a foreign policy achievement scored days before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
"I totally get why our official representatives need to 'play along' with the US first lady on Oleshky," said Artyom Sheynin, a prominent figure on Russian state TV.
"I understand why it's so important to create a 'success story' ahead of the elections for the US president, whose wife 'achieved a ceasefire' in Oleshky."
Kyiv, too, had its reasons to be fully compliant. Although relations with the US and its president are often fraught, Ukraine continues to rely heavily on US intelligence and US-made Patriot air defence missiles to counter Russian aerial attacks. Ahead of another tough winter of war, continued American support is essential to protect Ukrainian skies from Russia's assaults.
But though the ceasefire may have been born out of political calculation rather than purely humanitarian compassion, it also resulted in hundreds of civilians escaping.
There were emotional scenes when hundreds of Oleshky residentsarrived in northern Ukraine on Saturday. Many were met by tearful relatives they had not seen in years. To the journalists waiting, the evacuees told of years of hunger and hardship in a destroyed town.
The hundreds of residents who decided to stay behind will receive monthly humanitarian aid deliveries, Lantratova said, adding that decision too was the result of Melania Trump's mediation.
Yet the troop rotations and resupply efforts show that neither side is expecting Oleshky to be a blueprint for lasting respite in the future.
As Kherson came under fire again, Ukrainian drones hit several energy facilities across four Russian regions. In Samara, residents reported hearing explosions and seeing black plumes of smoke rising into the sky as an oil refinery was hit for the fifth time in a month.
If the truce brought a rare moment of relief to Oleshky, it has done little to alter the wider trajectory of a war that grinds on for now.

title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
summary: The food deal, ahead of a UK-EU summit later this month, is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far.
body:
The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month.
The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday.
Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders.
The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market.
The deal should remove the need for £200 Export Health Certificates, £25 Phytosanitary certificates, inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees, sampling fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU.
The government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen with Prime Minister Andy Burnham
UK exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes will also be able to resume.
The agreement will also allow for passports for UK pets taken into the EU.
Under the agreement the UK will commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards. This process is called "dynamic alignment".
While UK rules remain mostly aligned with EU ones, there are some areas where England has diverged from the EU rule book, for example on "precision breeding" of plants, previously known as gene editing. In recent weeks, agreement has been struck on transition arrangements while the EU's new regulations come in to force.
The government has already announced aEuropean Partnerships Billwhich will provide a legal mechanism for the application of new EU rules and regulations. This will also allow for the necessary alignments for the linking of the UK emissions trading scheme with the EU's, and save the need for UK exporters to pay the EU's new carbon border tax.
The draft agreements will be discussed at a meeting of EU ambassadors called Coreper on Wednesday, with some key details on the planned numbers in a Youth Experience Scheme to be finalised at a political level in the coming days. A discount on full foreign student fees for EU students is likely to be pushed to next year alongside a plan to reconnect electricity markets.
The BBC understands that the draft agreements will also include some references to UK involvement in defence cooperation schemes, access to law enforcement databases and some reassurances overthe EU's "Made in Europe" plans.
While the food trade plans have been backed by supermarkets and farmers representatives, some pro-Brexit campaigners have criticised the reapplication of EU rules. The post-Brexit trade deal signed by Boris Johnson's government prioritised regulatory freedoms for the UK over avoiding new regulatory red tape, checks and delays.
The British Chamber of Commerce released a new analysis of its members' views on Monday suggesting options for a closer relationship.
The business lobby group says the current trade relationship is "failing to deliver", leaving firms "struggling with a thicket of Brexit red tape" nearly six years after the UK's exit from the bloc.
It also pointed to economic analysis of more fundamental changes to the UK-EU relationship, suggesting the largest long-term economic boosts from rejoining the single market or the EU itself. The BCC called on government to analyse and publish options, as it consults its members.
The BCC is calling for an exploration of what a new relationship could look like, and offers nine options, including a customs union, a "Swiss-style" Single Market relationship, and a "Canada model" associate membership.
"The evidence from businesses suggests that the prime minister is right to have initiated a conversation on our future relationship with Europe, and he deserves real credit for having done so.
"Government needs to examine all of the options, remain clear-headed about the trade-offs each involves, and involve business in the decision-making process from the start," Shevaun Havilland, director general of the BCC, said.
More than half (56%) of exporting businesses in a BCC survey said they wanted EU customs paperwork and delays removed so they can grow. That rose to 58% of manufacturers.
The prime minister has said he wants to use this month's summit to launch a conversation on a longer term path for the UK's relationship with the EU, including "going all the way", meaning rejoining the bloc.

title: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
summary: The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C.
body:
'All this food is now useless': Piles of rubbish after shop freezers hit by cyber-attack
Dozens of supermarkets across sevenEuropean countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incidentthat hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.
Freezers have had to be emptied at several ICA grocery stores in Sweden after the cyber-attack
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".
He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.
Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.
"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.
The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).
It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.
In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.
Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.
In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost €100,000 (£83,500) worth of produce.
The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.
Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".
An employee at an ICA supermarket in Sweden's capital Stockholm was pictured throwing away bags of spoiled food
In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit.
A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".
"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.
One of the ICA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."
The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.
Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.
In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores.
The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.
The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.
In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.
A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.
A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.

title: North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack
summary: US government agencies and cyber analysts have blamed Pyongyang for the record-breaking heist.
body:
Kim Yo-jong, the sister of North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un
North Korea has denied claims that it was behind therecord $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance, calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".
Kim Yo-jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and thesister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history.
This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.
Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.
The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.
"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.
"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.
Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack
Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for athen-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybitin 2025.
Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said.
The country has consistently denied such claims.
Kim Yo-jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace".
Kim Yo-jong: North Korea's heir apparent?
Who is Kim Yo-jong? Video, 00:02:32Who is Kim Yo-jong?
The BBC has contacted Binance for comment. Since the hack, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users.
The company said initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals.
Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.
Binance said on Sunday that itscustomers pulled out more than $3.6bn of assetsfrom its exchange as it reopened after suspending all transactions in the wake of the hack.
The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach.

title: Apple unsure when more foldable iPhones will be available after selling out
summary: Apple’s foldable iPhone Duo was a hit with people willing to spend $2,000 on a new mobile.
body:
The new head of Apple says the company is working to get its new foldable iPhones available to more people after the$1,999 smartphonequickly sold out when it was released just over a week ago.
John Ternus, who in Septembertook over the roleas Apple's chief executive from Tim Cook, said on Monday that he was "thrilled" at the early reaction to the iPhone Duo.
While the costly phone, which sells for £1,999 in the UK, immediately sold out, some buyers have seen theirscreens crack.
The phones are still in high demand and Sabhi Kahn, Apple's new chief operating officer, said the technology giant did not know when more Duos would be available.
"At this time, it's really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance," Kahn said during a call with financial analysts to discuss Apple's latest financial results.
Apple executives did not mention during the call any issues with the iPhone Duo. But last week, the company said it would replace any phones that were impacted by an issue that caused a "small number" of the new phones to crack along the inside fold.
Nevertheless, Apple said on Monday that over the last year it sold more iPhones globally than it ever has before.
During the three months to 26 September, which did not include sales of the iPhone Duo that went on sale toward the end of October, Apple saw iPhone sales rise 17% to $57bn.
Apple has boasted throughout the year that iPhone sales have been surging, despite thecompany's warningsthat crucial components for the device, along with Mac computers and iPads, were constrained to the point of weighing down sales.
Sales of Mac computers also grew during the quarter by 27%, hitting $10.7bn, another record for Apple.
Overall sales at the company rose by 15% for the year, to $479bn.
However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and Watch fell by 10% and 7%, respectively.
Kahn noted during the call that most Apple devices are still seeing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with "advanced nodes."
Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allows Apple's devices to operate more quickly, most of which Apple has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan.
Khan said that such supply constraints are expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs. The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products.
Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of Apple devices to store data like apps, photos, and text messages.
Much of that memory storage runs through data centres which have seen a huge boom in demand for space as artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots and platforms, including those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic, have become popular.
As demand for memory has grown, storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple.
Cook had earlier this year referred to the sudden increase in data centre costs that Apple was seeing as a "thousand year flood."
It has led to the company raising prices on essentially all of its hardware products by around 20%.

title: Ryanair says it may freeze workers' pay and raise airfares
summary: The airline says fuel prices may rise by €2bn in 2028 unless there is an end to the US-Israel war with Iran.
body:
Ryanair is considering a temporary wage freeze for staff and confirmed airfares will be "materially higher" next summer because of a sharp rise in fuel costs following the US-Israel war with Iran.
The airline said it expects fuel prices to remain high "well into 2027" unless there is a "swift resolution" to the conflict.
Ryanair said its fuel bill is forecast to be €2bn (£1.6bn) higher in the short-term and its boss, Michael O'Leary, said airfares would have to rise by "double-digits" to help cover the cost.
But the firm said that was unlikely to be enough and it is looking into pay freezes. Unite, the union representing Ryanair staff, said it had not been told of "any such proposals".
O'Leary also said the company would slow down hiring as airline's costs rise.
The airline said its pre-tax profits fell by 16% to €2.4bn during the six months to the end of September, largely due to fuel costs jumping by 15%.
The company said that although 80% of its fuel bill had been "hedged" – in effect, bought in advance at fixed prices – the cost of the remainder was elevated.
O'Leary reiterated forecasts from earlier this year Ryanair would "need a 20% fare increase" to cover the cost of jet fuel.
"I'm not sure we'll get to 20%," he said. "But we're certainly looking at double-digit fare increases across Europe from all airlines in 2027."
Aviation fuel prices have surged this year as a result of the US-Israel war with Iran, which has dramatically reduced the supply of refined products coming from the Gulf and increased competition for those produced elsewhere.
Ryanair also said it was weighing up whether to freeze pay, as multi-year wage deals with unions come to to an end. The policy could be implemented from April next year.
Oliver Richardson, national officer at Unite, said the union "hasn't been advised of any such proposals and we have a multi-year pay deal in place which covers next year. A number of Unions across Europe have the same".
He said: "Our pay agreement was not attached to, nor dependent on company performance. This was something that the Ryanair was at pains to emphasise. As such we would expect it to be honoured."
Ryanair also said it would increase its use of artificial intelligence within its back office and support functions.
Meanwhile, Ryanair has cut back on winter flights and said on Monday there would be more to come. It said this was happening across the airline industry, particularly with short-haul carriers.
O'Leary said: "We believe those cuts will continue into the summer of 2027. Over the medium term, we expect short-haul capacity will remain constrained out to the early 2030s."

title: Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes
summary: Angela Rayner previously said plans were "un-British" and ministers shouldn't shift "the goalposts".
body:
Shabana Mahmood has backed down on two elements
Today's announcement has long been viewed in government as a potential political banana skin.
When the home secretary announced her first version of changes to the settlement system last year, many Labour MPs, including the housing secretary Angela Rayner, voiced their concerns about the plans.
But there was a feeling that Sir Keir Starmer's government was determined to plough on regardless. Shabana Mahmood herself repeatedly expressed how important she believed the reforms were.
But the change of prime minister over the summer gave renewed hope to those unhappy Labour MPs that they could force the Home Office into two changes.
Firstly, social care workers – under the original plans many social care workers would have had to wait 15 years before becoming eligible for settlement.
Secondly, the retrospective nature of the plans – some MPs were uncomfortable at the idea of someone coming to the UK and expecting to be eligible for settlement after five years, but then having to wait longer.
Angela Rayner described that as "un-British" and said the government shouldn't be shifting "the goalposts".
She returned to the cabinet under Andy Burnham as housing secretary and chose to repeat those criticisms in an interview during the Labour Party conference in September.
That was seen as evidence that a debate inside the top levels of government about whether to water down the plans was well and truly rumbling on.
For all the Labour MPs who wanted a change, there were others, particularly those in Brexit-supporting areas, who wanted the home secretary to stick the course.
Some inside government felt nervous about providing what they saw as catnip to Reform and the Conservatives.
All of that added up to one of the more difficult decisions that has had to be taken since Burnham walked through the doors of Number 10.
In the end ministers chose to water down the proposals for care workers – those who arrived before May 2025 and earn at least £25,000 a year will qualify for settlement in five years.
But the retrospective nature of the plans, the thing Rayner described as shifting "the goalposts", hasn't changed.
Despite that, the majority of Labour MPs pulled their punches whenMahmood made a statement in the House of Commons earlier.
Perhaps the strongest pushback came from Rachael Maskell, who is no fan of the retrospective element - but others on the left of the party, including John McDonnel and Diane Abbott, were critical without being scathing.
Mahmood scraps settlement plans for migrant care workers
What are the planned changes to immigration rules?
Outside the Commons chamber, the mood among Labour folk was pretty similar to what was said from the green benches.
One would-be critic said that while they personally still had concerns about the plans announced today, they believed the Home Secretary had successfully taken the political sting out of the situation for now.
They said the campaign by MPs and unions had led to a "big win" on settlement for social care workers, but said they were still expecting to hear from constituents negatively affected by the new rules.
One Number 10 source praised Mahmood's "take no prisoners" performance in the chamber, argued she had "found the right balance" and said the announcement had gone down as well as could be expected with Labour colleagues.
Of course, the home secretary will still need to deal with criticism from other parties.
Her opposite number for the Conservatives, Chris Philp, accused Mahmood of a significant U-turn.
Philp highlighted a claim she had previously made – that allowing care workers to reach settlement more quickly could cost the UK £10bn.
The social care workers plans announced todaywill see around 500,000 people have their path to settlement delayed, that number would have been around 800,000 under the original plans last year.
In an interview with the BBC, Mahmood wouldn't say what sort of financial burden her watering down would result in.
She also refused to confirm whether Burnham had directly asked her to water down the plans.
They are tricky questions that she will have to navigate over the coming weeks.
But the general view within government is that this is one political hurdle that has been successfully jumped.

title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
summary: The food deal, ahead of a UK-EU summit later this month, is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far.
body:
The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month.
The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday.
Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders.
The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market.
The deal should remove the need for £200 Export Health Certificates, £25 Phytosanitary certificates, inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees, sampling fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU.
The government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen with Prime Minister Andy Burnham
UK exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes will also be able to resume.
The agreement will also allow for passports for UK pets taken into the EU.
Under the agreement the UK will commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards. This process is called "dynamic alignment".
While UK rules remain mostly aligned with EU ones, there are some areas where England has diverged from the EU rule book, for example on "precision breeding" of plants, previously known as gene editing. In recent weeks, agreement has been struck on transition arrangements while the EU's new regulations come in to force.
The government has already announced aEuropean Partnerships Billwhich will provide a legal mechanism for the application of new EU rules and regulations. This will also allow for the necessary alignments for the linking of the UK emissions trading scheme with the EU's, and save the need for UK exporters to pay the EU's new carbon border tax.
The draft agreements will be discussed at a meeting of EU ambassadors called Coreper on Wednesday, with some key details on the planned numbers in a Youth Experience Scheme to be finalised at a political level in the coming days. A discount on full foreign student fees for EU students is likely to be pushed to next year alongside a plan to reconnect electricity markets.
The BBC understands that the draft agreements will also include some references to UK involvement in defence cooperation schemes, access to law enforcement databases and some reassurances overthe EU's "Made in Europe" plans.
While the food trade plans have been backed by supermarkets and farmers representatives, some pro-Brexit campaigners have criticised the reapplication of EU rules. The post-Brexit trade deal signed by Boris Johnson's government prioritised regulatory freedoms for the UK over avoiding new regulatory red tape, checks and delays.
The British Chamber of Commerce released a new analysis of its members' views on Monday suggesting options for a closer relationship.
The business lobby group says the current trade relationship is "failing to deliver", leaving firms "struggling with a thicket of Brexit red tape" nearly six years after the UK's exit from the bloc.
It also pointed to economic analysis of more fundamental changes to the UK-EU relationship, suggesting the largest long-term economic boosts from rejoining the single market or the EU itself. The BCC called on government to analyse and publish options, as it consults its members.
The BCC is calling for an exploration of what a new relationship could look like, and offers nine options, including a customs union, a "Swiss-style" Single Market relationship, and a "Canada model" associate membership.
"The evidence from businesses suggests that the prime minister is right to have initiated a conversation on our future relationship with Europe, and he deserves real credit for having done so.
"Government needs to examine all of the options, remain clear-headed about the trade-offs each involves, and involve business in the decision-making process from the start," Shevaun Havilland, director general of the BCC, said.
More than half (56%) of exporting businesses in a BCC survey said they wanted EU customs paperwork and delays removed so they can grow. That rose to 58% of manufacturers.
The prime minister has said he wants to use this month's summit to launch a conversation on a longer term path for the UK's relationship with the EU, including "going all the way", meaning rejoining the bloc.

title: PM plans debt re-set for Commonwealth nations as slavery apology talks begin
summary: The move comes as the prime minister begins talks about the UK issuing a formal apology for the slave trade in the next year.
body:
King Charles III with Prime Minister Andy Burnham at a Commonwealth Business Forum in Antigua
The prime minister will join the King at the formal opening of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua later - and begin talks with fellow leaders about the UK issuing a formal apology for the slave trade in the next year.
As part of the discussions, Downing Street said Andy Burnham would set out his plans for what it is calling a "debt reset" to support Commonwealth countries having to deal with the growing costs of paying interest on their debts.
The issue of reparations, compensation to those who were the victims of slavery, has dominated debate in the build up to this summit, in which representatives from 56 Commonwealth countries are meeting.
"Britain is bringing a new approach to this meeting," the prime minister said, in a tacit acknowledgement that the last Commonwealth gathering, on the Pacific island of Samoa two years ago, did not go well from a UK perspective.
The previous Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer had said prior to the meeting thatreparations were not on the agenda, but other leaders insisted they should be.
This time, the new prime minister has sought to get ahead of the debate, and appeared to directly address the anger of some Commonwealth leaders after the last summit.
"For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for anhonest conversation about the legacies of slavery,external. By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function," Burnham argued in an article in the Guardian.
Burnham alongside the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and the former Prime Minister Gordon Brown, are beginning conversations which, they hope, will help detoxify the debate about reparations.
They do so while insisting the UK will not pay them, but is likely to formally apologise for the slave trade for the first time next year, when the UK holds the rotating presidency of the G20 group of countries.
"A formal apology,"Miliband said in a social media video,external, is something "the British government are open to".
He said this would be a "significant step" but added that "we don't believe financial reparations are the right of feasible answer to transatlantic slavery. We don't think the right response is to ask British taxpayers today to make financial payments for these historic acts."
King's role is not policy making, says Palace in slavery apology row
No10 defends flight to Manchester to collect Andy Burnham
King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology
The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has urged the prime minister not to issue an apology for slavery, saying it would give countries a reason to ask the UK for reparations.
She said: "I don't think we should be giving any money to compensate people for the slave trade, and I don't think that Andy Burnham needs to be apologising because it is a lever to wedge open the door to ask for cash."
But British officials are hopeful, even confident, that the prime minister and foreign secretary's approach will create space in the next two days for a wider conversation with fellow Commonwealth countries.
No 10 said the UK would lead two new task forces - one focused on critical mineral assets and vulnerabilities in supply chains across the group and the other aimed at boosting trade and investment more widely.
Both will be set up by the end of the year and report back at the next leaders' summit, officials said.
British diplomats view the Commonwealth as a useful forum for conversations with developing countries, and, crucially, one that does not involve China, America or Russia.

title: Labour ends power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
summary: Labour's ruling National Executive Committee sets out where it is cutting ties with the Greens.
body:
The Greens have been in direct coalition with Labour on a handful of councils, including Sheffield
The Labour Party has pulled out of power-sharing agreements with the Green Party in 11 local councils, after the national party adopted a policy defining Zionism as a form of racism.
Labour councillors will no longer be in coalition with the Greens in areas including Sheffield, Warwick and Lewes.
Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson said: "Labour has been clear from the start that the "Zionism is Racism" policy crosses a line and we cannot work with any party that supports it – at any level of government."
Green leader Zack Polanski said the move would "backfire" on Labour and accused the party of wanting to "interrupt your local services and impose genocide support from it's local councils".
In October, Green Party members backed a motion, entitled "Zionism is racism", which said Zionism was an ideology that supported an "ethnonationalist Jewish State in historic Palestine". Israel has denied committing genocide in Gaza.
The motion also backed a "single democratic Palestinian State", including in modern-day Israel.
Having been backed by party members, the motion became Green Party policy, but it has left senior figuresbitterly divided. Jewish groups and opposition political parties have condemned it.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs in October that Labour would not partner with the Greens over the "antisemitic" policy.
Labour then issued an ultimatum from Labour's head office to Labour-Green councils, demanding that local Greens disown the motionpassed by membersat their national party conference.
Green groups were also asked to call on their party's national leadership to reconsider the policy.
Labour said there were local agreements in place in 18 authorities. Of those, Labour said 11 had not met the criteria it demanded.
Arun District Council
Derbyshire Dales District Council
Havant Borough Council
Lewes District Council (The Green Party announced last week it was "mutually" ending its alliance with Labour)
Runnymede Borough Council (Labour says local co-operation had already ceased)
Sheffield City Council
Stafford Borough Council
Warwick District Council
Wealden District Council
West Devon Borough Council
Labour said its conditions had been met in Broadland, Monmouthshire, North Somerset, Rother, West Oxfordshire and West Sussex. The party said that Coventry City Council does not have a formal arrangement in place and that no such deal will be made in the future.
It will continue co-operating with the Greens in the West of England mayoralty, where the deputy mayor is a Green member.
Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said the motion was "imperfect" but hasdefended its central premise, arguing that Israel's actions towards the Palestinian people are "clearly underpinned by racist ideology".
The collapse of co-operation at the local level could impact hundreds of thousands of residents through budgets and policy decisions taking longer to get voted through.
Green and Labour councillors in the impacted areas will now have to seek alternative coalition partners or try to govern as a minority administration.
In a joint statement, the Green Party and the Local Government Association Green Group said it was "hugely disappointed" that Labour had forced local leaders into "jeopardising successful progressive partnerships that are delivering benefits for residents".
One of the biggest councils to be affected is Sheffield, where 25 Labour councillors formed a power-sharing agreement with 20 Green councillors after the May 2026 elections for the Yorkshire city's 550,000 residents.
Responding to Labour's ultimatum, leader of the Sheffield Greens Angela Argenzio did not mention the motion in a letter but insisted local Green councillors "are not antisemitic".
Argenzio told local Labour representatives they were being "directed by your national party leader" rather than local concerns.
In a statement on Monday, the council's Labour leader Cllr Fran Belbin said her party would propose on Wednesday that it proceeds as a Labour minority administration.
"We now feel we are at the end of the road with the joint administration," she said.
"Our trust in Sheffield Greens is completely broken," she added, accusing them of a "refusal to stand up for Jewish citizens".
Green Party co-deputy leader Rachel Millward, also the leader of Wealden Council, said: "It is ironic that a Labour prime minister who made a promise to solve problems, not score points, has now shown he is willing to disrupt well-run councils for fear of Green success."
She added: "It is utterly irresponsible to conflate criticism of the actions of the state of Israel with antisemitism. Many Jewish people strongly reject the illegal actions of the current Israeli government."
In Warwick, the local Green party said: "We refuse to condemn a democratically decided policy because of political intimidation."
It urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to "reflect his own words in his actions and allow local Labour groups to decide for themselves".
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Green group leader in Havant Netty Shepherd accused Labour of "performative politics" and said the end of their coalition would be a "complete disaster for residents".
"I am a local government councillor, I worry about people's bins, I worry about generating town centres - foreign policy is nothing to do with my remit," she added.
The Liberal Democrats are also in partnership with the Green Party in some local councils.
Last week, the party leader Sir Ed Davey ruled out entering into a national partnership with "any party that is committed to a dangerous and antisemitic policy like the Green Party's".
He added that he had asked those of his local leaders in coalition with the Greens to urge Green councillors to reject the motion and commit to campaigning for its reversal.

title: MP Carla Lockhart quits DUP in Drumcree row
summary: Lockhart had called for the DUP to remove First Minister Michelle O'Neill from office.
body:
Carla Lockhart is the MP for Upper Bann, a seat she has held since 2019
Carla Lockhart has quit the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) in a row over its response to the Drumcree parading dispute.
The MP for Upper Bann had been calling for the party to withdraw Stormont's deputy first minister to force First Minister Michelle O'Neill from their joint office.
Lockhart said she was leaving the DUP on a "point of principle" and would continue in the House of Commons as an independent unionist.
The fall-out comes after unionist anger over Sinn Féin's involvement inprotests on Garvaghy Road, which blocked a contentious Orange Order parade from passing along the mainly nationalist street in Portadown, County Armagh.
O'Neill and several other senior Sinn Féin figures have beeninterviewed by policeinvestigating the demonstrations, with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.

Cutting links with a party she first joined as a teenager was a big call for Carla Lockhart.
Her family ties to the DUP run deep prompting one colleague to say, "Carla bleeds the DUP".
She has been on a collision course with the DUP leadership for weeks and now the "profound consequences" are being felt by the party.
Though she had some support within the DUP, she became a lone voice in her battle with the leadership.
She had the backing of Portadown Orangemen and many unionists, but Gavin Robinson crucially had the full support of the DUP officer and assembly teams.
He was able to face down the demands from his Upper Bann MP safe in the knowledge he had the numbers on his side.
Collapsing the executive without a budget agreed and running the risk of his party being blamed for a nurse's pay dispute strike was not a gamble he was willing to take.
But it has come at a cost for Robinson as he has now lost an MP from the DUP benches leaving just four for a party which once boasted ten members of parliament.
It has been a bruising time and one he needs to recover from quickly with just seven months until the assembly election.
